title: Rosh Hashanah: apples, honey, water
hookLine: sweet food for a sweet year, and crumbs cast into flowing water

cards: The shofar is serious. The table that night is sweet. On the eve of Rosh Hashanah, families sit down to a round challah, the braided bread shaped into a circle for a year that comes around again.
Someone passes apple slices and a small bowl of honey. You dip, and before you eat, you say a line many Jews have said for centuries: may it be God's will that this be a good and sweet year.
Then the next afternoon, something stranger: whole families standing on a riverbank, turning out their pockets.

teach.b: Start with the table. The Talmud mentions foods eaten at the new year as good signs, things that grow quickly or come in abundance. Over time, communities built whole menus around wordplay.

Pomegranates, for merits as many as their seeds. In some homes, the head of a fish, to be the head and not the tail. Dates, carrots, leeks and beets, because their Hebrew or Yiddish names sound like wishes.

teach.h: APPLES AND HONEY: A SWEET YEAR.
teach.b: Apples and honey are simply the best known: sweetness, said out loud. Then comes the water.
On the first afternoon of Rosh Hashanah, many Jews walk to a river, a stream, a lake or the sea, anywhere the water moves and, ideally, fish live.

teach.h: CAST INTO THE DEPTHS OF THE SEA.
teach.b: They read verses from the prophet Micah, which end with a picture of God's mercy: "And Thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea." The ceremony is named for that word, cast: tashlich, you will cast.
Many bring bread crumbs and toss them in, one crumb for each thing they want to leave behind. Here's the honest part. Tashlich isn't in the Torah or the Talmud.

It shows up in Germany in the late Middle Ages, and some rabbis were uneasy with it, worried people would think crumbs in a river could wash away sins by themselves. Jewish teaching is clear that they can't.
The work of changing belongs to the Days of Awe, the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur.
Tashlich is a picture of that work, not a substitute for it.
But what a picture: you stand at moving water, and you let something go.

how: On Rosh Hashanah eve, many Jewish families eat apples dipped in honey and a round challah, often with other symbolic foods. On the first afternoon, many go to flowing water for tashlich, reading verses from Micah and sometimes tossing crumbs.

o: a blessing said over apples and honey
a fast day of repentance before the new year
you will cast: letting go at moving water

games.why: tashlich is done at moving or natural water, ideally where fish live, reading the verses from Micah.

practice: Name, silently, one thing you'd like to leave behind this year: a habit, a grudge, a way you talked to someone.
Picture holding it in your hand like a crumb, then picture moving water, a river, a fountain, even a sink with the tap running, and watch it float away.
